name: Oil Yellow
lede: Oil Yellow is a light, greenish yellow from Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary, first recorded on their chip in 1843, decades before the dictionary itself was published.

sections.title: A chip dated to 1843
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930) places this color at plate 12, chip L1, and dates the chip's first record to 1843, nearly ninety years before the book appeared [1]. The ISCC-NBS system did not coin a separate name; it only classifies the chip as a light greenish yellow [1]. Our library notes a later synonym on a nearby chip, Liqueur Green, first recorded in 1927 [2].

In our color graph its closest named relatives are [[lumiere-green]], duller, and [[siskin-green]], also duller, with [[citronelle]] and [[june-bud]], both more vivid, close behind [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, a color within six units of Oil Yellow covers at least five per cent of a canvas in only 17 works, rarer than 64 per cent of our named colors [4]. It peaks in the 1800s, in 9 of 8,345 paintings, found in 0.1 per cent of our paintings from that century, 1.6 times the archive's overall rate [4]. The earliest dated appearance in our archive is 1642, about two centuries before the 1930 dictionary recorded it, a look-alike hue, not proof of pigment, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [4]. These remain photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors [4].
